public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Normality of Irrational Algebraic Numbers

It is unknown whether every irrational algebraic real number is normal in any integer base.
Here a real number is *normal in base* $b$ if, for every $k \ge 1$, every string of $k$ digits
appears in its base-$b$ expansion with asymptotic frequency $1/b^k$.
The stronger conjecture that every irrational algebraic real number is absolutely normal is stated
separately: normality in one base and normality in every base are not equivalent definitions.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia: Normal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_number)
- [BC01] Bailey, David H., and Richard E. Crandall. "On the random character of fundamental constant
  expansions." Experimental Mathematics 10.2 (2001): 175-190.
  https://projecteuclid.org/journals/experimental-mathematics/volume-10/issue-2/On-the-random-character-of-fundamental-constant-expansions/em/999188630.full
-/

@[expose] public section

open NormalNumber

namespace AlgebraicNormality

/-- A real number is irrational algebraic if it is algebraic over `ℚ` but not rational. -/
def IsIrrationalAlgebraic (x : ℝ) : Prop :=
  IsAlgebraic ℚ x ∧ Irrational x

/-- The strong normality conjecture: every irrational algebraic real is absolutely normal. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11 12 41]
theorem irrational_algebraic_absolutely_normal :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ x : ℝ, IsIrrationalAlgebraic x → IsAbsolutelyNormal x := by
  sorry

/-- The weaker normality conjecture: every irrational algebraic real is normal in at least one
integer base `b ≥ 2`. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11 12 41]
theorem irrational_algebraic_normal_in_some_base :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      ∀ x : ℝ, IsIrrationalAlgebraic x → ∃ b : ℕ, 2 ≤ b ∧ IsNormalInBase b x := by
  sorry

/-- Absolute normality implies normality in at least one base. -/
@[category API, AMS 11]
theorem normal_in_some_base_of_absolutely_normal {x : ℝ} (hx : IsAbsolutelyNormal x) :
    ∃ b : ℕ, 2 ≤ b ∧ IsNormalInBase b x :=
  ⟨2, le_rfl, hx 2 le_rfl⟩

end AlgebraicNormality

reformulations.difference: The shared IsNormalInBase definition includes zero-length words and counts occurrences starting at i < n, whereas the source describes positive-length blocks wholly contained in the first n digits.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For length zero the count is n, so its frequency tends to 1, exactly the required value. For each fixed positive length k, counting all starting positions below n instead of only blocks contained in the first n digits changes the count by at most k−1; after division by n this difference tends to zero. In /workspace/review/scratch.lean, normal_iff_source_normal proves equivalence of these normality definitions, and absolute_conjecture_iff_source propagates it through the conjecture’s quantifiers. Neither proof depends on sorryAx.

reformulations.difference: This weaker variant uses the same zero-length-inclusive, starting-position counting convention rather than counting positive-length blocks contained in each sampled prefix.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The empty-word condition is automatic, and the two positive-length frequency sequences differ by a quantity tending to zero. Their equivalence holds for every base and real number, so it remains valid under ∃ b : ℕ, 2 ≤ b ∧ … and the outer quantification over irrational algebraic reals. The theorem some_base_conjecture_iff_source in /workspace/review/scratch.lean proves this equivalence without sorryAx.

review.notes: Checked all four declarations. The absolute-normality conjecture matches both mathematical sources; the some-base statement is explicitly labelled as a weaker variant, not an equivalent replacement. The irrational-algebraic hypothesis is satisfiable (verified with √2) and excludes rationals. Boundary tests covered exact digit extraction, negative inputs, integer translations, n=0, empty words, and the degenerate bases 0 and 1, which both conjectures correctly exclude. The API theorem correctly selects base 2. Both research-open tags agree with Wikipedia. The cited Project Euclid endpoint was blocked; the paper was read through the author-hosted manuscript instead.
